stem: Which developmental feature best explains why infants and young children are prone to ventilation–perfusion mismatch during acute respiratory illness?
explanation: Fewer alveoli is the correct answer. Infants and young children have fewer alveoli, which increases the potential for ventilation–perfusion mismatch during acute respiratory illness.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Respiratory 3.1 Acute Respiratory Problems

optionExplanations.A: Correct because fewer alveoli reduce the respiratory surface area and contribute to ventilation–perfusion mismatch.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because a large occiput affects head positioning and airway alignment, not alveolar number or ventilation–perfusion matching.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because the cricoid cartilage being narrowest is an airway anatomy feature, not the reason for ventilation–perfusion mismatch.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because a longer epiglottis is an anatomical feature of the upper airway, not a cause of ventilation–perfusion mismatch.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because a higher resting respiratory rate is a physiological characteristic, not the developmental feature that explains ventilation–perfusion mismatch.
